findings.requirement_type: D&O — Manufacturing & Professional Services Exclusion (Core-Operations Bar)
findings.contract_quote: To the fullest extent permitted by law... the contractor shall defend, indemnify, and hold harmless the County... from and against all claims, damages, losses, and expenses... arising out of, or alleged to have resulted from, the negligent acts, errors, omissions, or mistakes relating to the performance of this contract...
findings.policy_quote: EXCLUSION FOR MANUFACTURING AND PROFESSIONAL SERVICE ENDORSEMENT... bars D&O coverage for any Claim based upon, arising from, or in any way related to: (1) malfunction of any product or product failure due to deficiency/inadequacy/defect/dangerous condition in product or its design/manufacture; or (2) rendering or failure to render any services for fees (including services for customers/clients).
findings.policy_page: Endorsement #19 (Form PP 00 H350 00 0616), Page 85 of Hartford Mgmt Liability
findings.gap_description: The Hartford Private Choice Premier D&O coverage part contains a near-absolute exclusion barring entity coverage for any claim arising from product failure or rendering/failing to render services for fees. For Run-Test Election Services — whose entire business is rendering ballot printing, mail processing, and election technology services for fees to county clients — this exclusion eliminates D&O Side B (corporate reimbursement) and Side C (entity) coverage for the most realistic claim scenarios: a county suing the entity for service-delivery failures, ballot errors, or election-mail mishandling. Carve-backs only preserve coverage for shareholder-driven civil proceedings and derivative actions, which are unlikely scenarios for a private, PE-backed company.
findings.plain_english: Your D&O policy has a clause that says it won't pay for lawsuits that come from your products failing or from the services you provide your customers. Since literally everything your business does is provide services to county clients, this exclusion gutted the most useful part of the policy. If Maricopa or Sacramento sues the company for a ballot processing error, your D&O policy is unlikely to respond. Personal claims against directors and officers are still covered (Side A), but the company itself is largely on its own.
findings.recommendation: At renewal, market the D&O to carriers that do not impose a manufacturing/professional services exclusion (Chubb, AIG, Travelers Bond all have alternative forms for this risk profile). If staying with Hartford, push hard for endorsement removal or a carve-back for derivative actions arising from service failures. In the interim, ensure E&O is structured to pick up the operational claims gap.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: Partial — operational service failures may fall to Tech E&O ($10M tower); but D&O-style allegations against directors/officers personally for failure to oversee operations remain narrowly covered under Side A only.
discoveryQuestions: When you renewed your Management Liability policy, did anyone walk you through the 'Manufacturing and Professional Services' exclusion on page 85? Do you understand which kinds of lawsuits it actually blocks?
If a county sued Runbeck for negligent mail processing or a ballot defect, who at the company would expect the D&O policy to defend them — and what would happen when they found out it doesn't?

Your private equity sponsors sit on the board. If they were named individually in a county lawsuit alleging the company mismanaged election services, do you know whether their personal defense would even be triggered under this policy?
Have you priced D&O markets that don't impose this exclusion on election services firms? What was the premium delta?

findings.requirement_type: Cyber Liability — Limit Shortfall vs. Maricopa Spec
findings.contract_quote: Cyber, Network Security and Privacy Liability Insurance with a limit of not less than $5,000,000 per occurrence. The policy shall include, but not be limited to; coverage for all directors, officers, agents and employees of the Contractor, losses with respect to network risks (such as data breaches, unauthorized access or use, and ID theft of data), invasion of privacy... regulatory defense costs plus fines and penalties, cyber extortion, electronic data restoration expenses... network business interruption, computer fraud coverage, funds transfer loss, third-party fidelity...
findings.policy_quote: Aggregate Limit of Liability: $4,000,000... DEFENSE COSTS ARE PART OF AND NOT IN ADDITION TO THE AGGREGATE LIMIT OF LIABILITY. THE AGGREGATE LIMIT OF LIABILITY AVAILABLE TO PAY LOSS AND THE RETENTION SHALL BE REDUCED AND MAY BE EXHAUSTED BY THE PAYMENT OF DEFENSE COSTS.
findings.gap_description: Maricopa County requires $5,000,000 PER OCCURRENCE cyber. The AmTrust Cyber program is structured as a single $4,000,000 AGGREGATE limit shared across 14 coverage lines (Ransom, Data Recovery, Bricking, BI, BI from Suppliers, Reputation Harm, Cyber Event, Cyber Deception, Proof of Loss, Cryptojacking, Privacy & Network Security, Regulatory Fines, Payment Card, Media), with defense within limits. Three compounding shortfalls vs. the contract: (1) limit is $4M not $5M; (2) limit is aggregate not per-occurrence; (3) defense erodes the limit so effective indemnity capacity on a real claim is roughly $800K–$1.6M after typical 60–80% defense burn. The Hanover Umbrella does NOT follow form to Cyber (475-0654/0655/0661 cyber and data privacy exclusions), so there is no excess capacity to bridge the gap.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa County's contract requires $5 million in cyber insurance for each cyber event. You carry $4 million total for the entire policy year — and that $4 million has to pay defense lawyers, forensic firms, breach coaches, AND any settlements out of the same bucket. By the time defense is spent (typically 60-80% of the recovery on cyber claims), you have about $800K–$1.6M left for an actual claim payout. Your umbrella does not extend over cyber. So you are technically in breach of the Maricopa contract on day one of the policy, and your real-world cyber capacity for a major incident is roughly one-fifth of what the contract demands. For a company holding 90 million voter records, this is the single largest insurance gap in the program.
findings.recommendation: Three immediate actions: (1) increase the AmTrust Cyber primary to $5M minimum (or replace with a carrier that offers $5M per-occurrence not aggregate); (2) add a $5M excess Cyber tower to reach a true $10M aggregate, restoring meaningful capacity after defense erosion; (3) negotiate defense outside the limits at the next renewal — multiple cyber markets (Beazley, AIG, CFC) offer this. Stop-gap option: explore captive participation for the bottom layer to align internal capital with the contractual requirement.
discoveryQuestions: When you sit across from the Maricopa County Risk Manager and they ask you to certify $5M per-occurrence cyber, how do you plan to explain the $4M aggregate?
If you suffered a $2M ransomware event in October, then a wire fraud loss in February, and a regulatory fine notice in March — how much capacity would you have left for the regulatory defense?

Has your CFO modeled what an actual breach of 90 million voter records would cost in notification, credit monitoring, regulatory fines across 31 states, and shareholder/customer litigation? How does that compare to $4M?
What conversations have you had with your cyber broker about why this program was sized to $4M and not $10M or $15M?

findings.requirement_type: Cyber — Deception/Social Engineering Phantom Coverage
findings.contract_quote: ...computer fraud coverage, funds transfer loss, third-party fidelity, theft, no requirement for arrest and conviction, and loss outside the premises of the named insured.
findings.policy_quote: Cyber Deception (Social Engineering): Limit $250,000 / Retention $250,000
findings.policy_page: AmTrust Cyber Dec page Item 7, p 3
findings.gap_description: The Cyber Deception (social engineering) sublimit is $250,000 with a $250,000 retention. The math: a $300,000 wire fraud loss recovers $50,000. A $500,000 loss recovers $250,000 (50%). Any loss at or below $250,000 is fully retained — zero indemnity. This is functionally phantom coverage. Hartford Crime within the Management Liability bundle adds a separate Deception Fraud / Social Engineering sublimit of only $15,000. Total program social engineering capacity is therefore $265,000 — wholly inadequate for an election services vendor processing county invoices, vendor payables, and real-estate closings tied to PE-sponsor entities.
findings.plain_english: If a fraudster impersonating a county finance officer tricks one of your AP staff into wiring $400,000, your cyber policy will pay $150,000 of that loss. If they trick you into wiring $200,000, the policy pays nothing. The retention equals the limit, which makes the coverage almost useless. Combined with the $15,000 social engineering sublimit on your Crime policy, the program covers roughly a quarter-million in social engineering — a small fraction of what wire fraud claims actually cost a company your size.
findings.recommendation: Buy back full social engineering coverage at the $5M cyber tower limit, or add a standalone Crime form with $1M+ Computer Fraud / Funds Transfer Fraud / Social Engineering. Make the retention align with normal cyber retention ($25K-$50K), not the limit. Implement dual-control payment authorization and out-of-band verification protocols as a precondition for higher limits.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: Hartford ML Crime — Deception Fraud sublimit only $15,000 (Crime Dec, page 8); Hartford Crime Computer/Funds Transfer Fraud at $2M may respond if loss meets the strict 'fraudulent entry' definition rather than 'fraudulent instruction', but is not designed for social-engineering wire fraud.
discoveryQuestions: Walk me through your AP team's process when an invoice arrives from one of your county clients changing wire instructions. What happens when the email looks legitimate?
Did the broker explain to you that the $250K Cyber Deception sublimit pays nothing on the first $250K of any social engineering loss?
Have you had any near-miss social engineering events in the last three years that didn't result in a loss? What did you learn from them?
If a county AP department got socially engineered to redirect a $400K Runbeck payment to a fraudster, would Runbeck be on the hook to make the county whole? What would your insurance pay?

findings.requirement_type: Cyber — Additional Insured / Waiver of Subrogation / P&NC Missing
findings.contract_quote: The insurance policies required by this contract, except Workers' Compensation and Errors and Omissions, shall name County, its agents, representatives, officers, directors, officials, and employees as additional insureds... The policies required hereunder, except Workers' Compensation and Errors and Omissions, shall contain a waiver of transfer of rights of recovery (subrogation) against County... Contractor's insurance shall be primary insurance as respects County, and any insurance or self-insurance maintained by County shall not contribute to it.
findings.policy_quote: [No Additional Insured, Waiver of Subrogation, or Primary & Noncontributory endorsement visible in the AmTrust Cyber policy structure or Item 8 endorsement schedule]
findings.policy_page: AmTrust Cyber CYDECS 0122, p 2-4 (Item 8 Endorsements list blank in extracted text)
findings.gap_description: Maricopa County's contract carve-out of AI/WoS/P&NC requirements is limited to WC and E&O — Cyber is therefore in scope and must carry all three endorsements. The AmTrust Cyber policy as documented carries none. Many cyber forms do not accommodate AI status by carrier underwriting standards (the assumption being that cyber is a first-party-heavy form), and AmTrust may simply not endorse AI on the form. P&NC and WoS are typically endorsable. As of policy inception 4/1/2025, this is an uncured contract breach exposing Run-Test to declaratory relief, contract termination, and indemnity exposure to Maricopa for any loss the county would otherwise have recovered against Runbeck's cyber tower.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa County requires you to add the County as an Additional Insured on your cyber policy and to waive your insurer's right to chase the County for any losses. Your cyber policy doesn't have either endorsement. This is a contractual breach the day the contract takes effect. The County could refuse to issue work orders, demand correction, or — in a worst case — terminate for cause. More importantly, if the County itself is named in a breach lawsuit involving Runbeck's data, the County would expect to defend itself under Runbeck's policy; without AI status, the County looks to its own coverage and then back at Runbeck for indemnity.
findings.recommendation: Within 30 days, request from AmTrust: (1) blanket-by-contract Additional Insured endorsement on Cyber (or scheduled endorsements naming Maricopa, Sacramento, and LA County); (2) blanket Waiver of Subrogation; (3) Primary & Noncontributory wording. If AmTrust will not endorse, market to a cyber carrier that will (Chubb, Tokio Marine HCC, and several others routinely add these). Sacramento §VII.A also requires AI on 'liability arising out of activities performed by or on behalf of the CONTRACTOR' — confirm scope when adding.
discoveryQuestions: Have any of your county clients ever asked for a certificate of insurance specifically naming them as an Additional Insured on cyber? What did your broker do?
If Maricopa County is sued as a co-defendant in a breach involving voter data Runbeck processed, how do you envision the County getting defended — through its own policy or yours?
Has AmTrust confirmed in writing that they will issue an Additional Insured endorsement on this cyber form? If they won't, do you know which carriers will?
When was the last time someone audited the contract requirements against the actual endorsements on your cyber policy?

findings.requirement_type: Tech E&O — Split Limits Endorsement Cuts Coverage on Older Acts
findings.contract_quote: PROFESSIONAL LIABILITY OR ERRORS AND OMISSIONS LIABILITY: $1,000,000 per claim and aggregate.
findings.policy_quote: Limits of Liability... (a) Acts on or after Retro Date 12/1/2007: $1M each claim / $1M aggregate; (b) Acts on or after 09/06/2019: additional $1M xs $1M each claim / $1M xs $1M aggregate; (c) Acts on or after 04/01/2021: additional $3M xs $2M each claim / $3M xs $2M aggregate.
findings.policy_page: Endorsement #4 (Form AD 66 16 04 09 — Split Limits of Liability), p 22
findings.gap_description: The Gemini primary Tech E&O is structured as $5M/$5M on the Dec page, but Endorsement #4 replaces the limit section with a tiered structure. Wrongful Acts first committed before 9/6/2019 carry only $1M/$1M of coverage; acts before 4/1/2021 carry only $2M/$2M. The full $5M/$5M tower applies only to acts first committed on or after 4/1/2021. The Convex follow-form excess sits over this tiered structure and inherits its limitations (XPL-300 §I 'follows the more restrictive provisions'). Run-Test has been operating for 50+ years; latent claims emerging from pre-2019 work — historic election cycles, long-term software/hardware, prior county contracts — are limited to $1M total. For an election services vendor where claim emergence often lags actual events by years (recount lawsuits, post-election certification disputes), this is a material structural limit defect, not a paperwork issue.
findings.plain_english: Your $5M/$5M E&O policy looks like $5M/$5M on the front page. But buried in Endorsement #4, the policy says: if the underlying mistake happened before September 2019, you only get $1M of coverage; if it happened before April 2021, you only get $2M. You only get the full $5M for things that went wrong on or after April 1, 2021. For an election services company that has been processing ballots for half a century, a lot of latent claims could emerge from older work — and you'd be looking at one-fifth of the limit you think you bought.
findings.recommendation: Negotiate at renewal to collapse the split-limits structure into a flat $5M/$5M tied to the 3/27/2017 retro date — or move the program to a carrier that doesn't impose tiered limits. Pricing impact may be modest. If the carrier won't budge, document specifically which contracts/services pre-date 9/6/2019 and 4/1/2021 so you can quantify the residual exposure.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: Convex excess follows form and inherits the same tiered limits — does NOT cure the gap.
discoveryQuestions: Did anyone explain to you that your $5M E&O policy actually pays only $1M for mistakes that happened before September 2019?
Of the county contracts you currently service, how many were active and performing services before April 2021? What was the size of those engagements?
Election lawsuits sometimes don't emerge until two or three election cycles later. If a 2020-cycle ballot processing error surfaced in a 2026 lawsuit, do you know which limit tier would apply?
What would the premium be to flatten this to a true $5M/$5M with no tiering? Has your broker quoted it?

findings.requirement_type: Tech E&O — Mail Processing Has Narrower Retro Date
findings.contract_quote: If professional liability coverage is written on a Claims Made form: A. The 'Retro Date' must be shown, and must be on or before the date of the Agreement or the beginning of Agreement performance by CONTRACTOR.
findings.policy_quote: Specific Professional Service Retroactive Date: 04/01/2021 (instead of policy Retro 03/27/2017) applies specifically to 'outbound and inbound mail processing services.'
findings.policy_page: Endorsement #1 (Form VP 07 84 07 17 — Specific Professional Service Retroactive Date), p 19
findings.gap_description: The base policy retro is 3/27/2017, but Endorsement #1 carves out 'outbound and inbound mail processing services' — Run-Test's largest single service line — and resets its retro to 4/1/2021. Mail processing claims arising from acts pre-4/1/2021 are uninsured. This is a deliberate underwriter narrowing of the most claim-prone service. Sacramento §V.A requires retro 'on or before the date of the Agreement or the beginning of Agreement performance' — and Run-Test has been performing mail processing for counties for far longer than 4/1/2021. Any latent mail processing error from pre-2021 contracts is uncovered; the contract is technically out of compliance for any Sacramento agreement that pre-dates 4/1/2021 or that contemplates mail processing performed under prior arrangements.
findings.plain_english: Your E&O policy has one retro date for most of your business (March 2017) and a different, much later retro date (April 2021) just for mail processing — your single biggest service line. Anything that went wrong with a piece of election mail before April 2021 is not covered, regardless of when the lawsuit shows up. For a company that has been processing election mail for decades, that is a meaningful pre-existing gap — and it doesn't comply with Sacramento's contract language requiring retro coverage 'on or before' the start of contract performance.
findings.recommendation: At renewal, negotiate removal of Endorsement #1 — either eliminating the carve-out or pushing the mail-processing retro back to match the base policy retro of 3/27/2017. If the carrier insists on the carve-out, evaluate whether a competing carrier will offer single-retro coverage. Document all county contracts where Run-Test's mail processing performance pre-dates 4/1/2021 and disclose the carve-out in good faith to the County Risk Managers.
discoveryQuestions: How long has Runbeck been processing election mail for county clients before April 2021?
When the carrier added the April 2021 retro for mail processing, did the broker explain why — was there a specific incident or claim history that triggered that?
Is there any county currently sending you mail-processing claims or complaints related to work performed before April 2021?
If a 2019 ballot mail incident emerged as a lawsuit today, would Runbeck be paying defense costs out of pocket?

findings.requirement_type: Tech E&O — Client Print Media Exclusion (County-Furnished Content)
findings.contract_quote: PROFESSIONAL LIABILITY OR ERRORS AND OMISSIONS LIABILITY: $1,000,000 per claim and aggregate.
findings.policy_quote: Client Print Media: EXCLUDES Claims by clients of the Insured if Claim is a result of print media or Content furnished BY the client.
findings.gap_description: The Tech E&O Media Extension introduces an exclusion for claims by clients arising from print media or content furnished by the client. In Run-Test's business model, COUNTIES typically furnish ballot content, voter rolls, candidate data, election proposition language, etc. — Run-Test prints what counties supply. When a county sues Run-Test for a ballot defect, the litigation will turn on whether the defect was in Run-Test's printing/processing or in the underlying content the county furnished. The exclusion gives the carrier room to deny coverage for the very claims the policy is meant to insure. There is no carve-back for printing errors in client-furnished content.
findings.plain_english: Almost every county you work for sends you the ballot data, candidate lists, and proposition language — you print what they give you. Your E&O policy now excludes any claim from a client that arises from materials they furnished to you. If Maricopa sues you over a misprinted ballot, the carrier can argue that because the underlying data came from the County, the claim is excluded. Even if you printed it perfectly per their data, the exclusion gives the insurer wiggle room to deny. This is exactly the kind of exclusion that doesn't bother you until you have a claim.
findings.recommendation: Before next renewal, push for a specific carve-back: 'Exclusion W shall not apply to the extent the alleged error or omission relates to the Insured's printing, mail processing, or fulfillment services performed on client-furnished content.' Alternatively, market to a Tech E&O carrier without this exclusion. Document with each county contract that Run-Test's services include accurate reproduction of furnished content but not verification of underlying data — this becomes an allocation argument later.
discoveryQuestions: Walk me through what happens when Maricopa sends you the ballot file for a primary election. Who supplies the layout, the text, the voter database?
If a candidate's name was misspelled on a ballot you printed, how would the lawsuit allocate fault between the County's data and your printing?
Did the broker explain that Endorsement W of your E&O policy specifically excludes claims from clients arising from materials they furnished to you?
Have you ever had a claim or near-miss where a county blamed Runbeck for a problem in content they originally supplied?

findings.requirement_type: Tech E&O — Delay In Performance Exclusion
findings.contract_quote: PROFESSIONAL LIABILITY OR ERRORS AND OMISSIONS LIABILITY: $1,000,000 per claim and aggregate.
findings.policy_quote: Delay in Performance/Delivery: Excludes delay claims for Technology Products/services/contractual obligations.
findings.policy_page: Endorsement #6 (Technology Services Extension), Item D, p 26
findings.gap_description: The Tech E&O Technology Services Extension excludes claims arising from delay in performance or delivery of technology products/services/contractual obligations. Election work is fundamentally time-critical — ballots must be printed and mailed by statutory deadlines, scanners must be tested and operational by election day, results must be processed within certification windows. Late delivery is one of the highest-likelihood claim scenarios for any election services vendor. The exclusion eliminates coverage for the most foreseeable claim type. There is no carve-back tied to the cause of the delay (e.g., supply chain, equipment failure, force majeure are all swept into the exclusion).
findings.plain_english: If you miss a ballot delivery deadline because of a printer breakdown, a paper supply issue, or a postal slowdown, and a county sues you for the cost of emergency mailing, lost confidence, or election damages — your E&O policy says no coverage. Election work runs on hard statutory deadlines. Delay claims aren't theoretical for an election services vendor; they are one of the most predictable failure modes. This exclusion takes out exactly the risk the carrier should be covering.
findings.recommendation: Negotiate carve-back at renewal: delays caused by negligence in performance of Professional Services should remain covered, with only true contractual schedule overruns excluded. If carrier won't budge, market to other Tech E&O carriers (Chubb, Tokio Marine HCC, Beazley write election technology). At minimum, document business continuity protocols (redundant printers, alternative carriers, backup facilities) to reduce the likelihood of a delay claim.
discoveryQuestions: What is the busiest week of your year, and what's the worst-case scenario if a key piece of equipment fails on Tuesday morning before a Tuesday-night ballot mail-out?
If a county had to spend $200,000 on overnight USPS to recover a Runbeck delay, what would happen when they sent you the bill?
Did the broker walk you through the 'Delay in Performance' exclusion in your E&O policy, and explain that it applies even if the delay was caused by your own negligence?
Have you had a near-miss where a delay almost became a lawsuit? What did it cost to recover?

findings.requirement_type: Tech E&O — Network Security & Privacy Breach Exclusion (Privacy Risk Pushed to Cyber)
findings.contract_quote: PROFESSIONAL LIABILITY OR ERRORS AND OMISSIONS LIABILITY: $1,000,000 per claim and aggregate.
findings.policy_quote: Network Security, Privacy Breach and Biometric Identifiers or Biometric Information Exclusions... excludes from Professional Liability any Claim arising from data breach, network security failure, mishandling of confidential/personal information, GLBA, HIPAA, FTC §5(a), DPPA, CA SB 1386 violations.
findings.gap_description: The Tech E&O excludes any claim arising from data breach, network security failure, mishandling of confidential/personal information, or biometric data violations — these claims must come exclusively from a separate Cyber policy. Combined with the AmTrust Cyber's $4M shared aggregate (Finding 002), Run-Test has effectively no E&O fallback for privacy claims; everything is concentrated on the underpowered Cyber tower. The exclusion is appropriate insurance market structure (E&O insures professional negligence; Cyber insures privacy/security), but it amplifies the criticality of fixing the Cyber tower size.
findings.plain_english: Your E&O policy specifically says it won't pay for any claim involving a data breach, voter data exposure, or privacy violation — those go to the Cyber policy. That's normal in the insurance market. The problem is that your Cyber policy is undersized. So when the E&O kicks the privacy claims over to Cyber, Cyber doesn't have the limits to absorb them. The two policies, designed to work together, leave a gap because one of them is too small.
findings.recommendation: This finding is the structural counter-weight to Finding 002. Sizing the Cyber tower to $10M cures both findings simultaneously. Do not negotiate this exclusion off the E&O — it's a feature, not a bug, and removing it would price the E&O dramatically higher.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: AmTrust Cyber — but the Cyber tower itself is undersized (see Finding 002).
discoveryQuestions: Do you understand the deliberate handoff between your E&O and Cyber policies — that privacy claims go only to Cyber?
If a class action emerged from a voter PII breach, which policy do you expect to defend, and which would the lawyers be invoicing first?
Has anyone modeled a scenario where the E&O and the Cyber both deny — saying 'it's the other policy's problem'?

findings.requirement_type: Hartford D&O / EPLI / Fiduciary — Prior Acts Cutoff at 8/18/2023 (1-Year Window)
findings.contract_quote: If the insurance required is written on a claims-made basis, Contractor warrants that any retroactive date under the policy shall precede the effective date of this contract...
findings.policy_quote: Prior Acts Exclusion: Excludes Claims based upon/arising from/related to any Wrongful Act prior to 8/18/2023, or Interrelated Wrongful Acts thereto. Applies to D&O, EPLI AND Fiduciary.
findings.gap_description: The Hartford Management Liability bundle has a hard prior-acts exclusion at 8/18/2023 — applied across D&O, EPLI, AND Fiduciary. Policy effective is 8/18/2024, so the prior-acts window is exactly one year. Run-Test has 50+ years of operating history, has been PE-backed for some period prior, and has had multiple county contracts in force well before 8/18/2023. Any latent claim arising from acts before 8/18/2023 — a discrimination claim from 2022, an ERISA fiduciary breach from 2020, a 2019 election-cycle securities-style claim, a board-decision claim from before the prior-acts cutoff — is uninsured. The Endorsement #34 split prior-or-pending date for the upper $1M D&O layer (4/2/2024) further narrows the upper-layer coverage. CLAUDE.md flags this exact pattern as a heightened concern for PE-backed companies.
findings.plain_english: Your Management Liability policy only covers wrongful acts that happened on or after August 18, 2023. Anything before that — board decisions made years ago, an HR matter from 2022, fiduciary moves from before the PE buyout — is excluded. Your company has been operating for fifty-plus years; this one-year window leaves enormous historical exposure uninsured. PE-backed companies face heightened regulatory and litigation scrutiny precisely about decisions made BEFORE the prior-acts date.
findings.recommendation: At renewal, push hard for full prior-acts coverage retroactive to the date of incorporation or, at minimum, predating any active county contracts and the PE acquisition closing date. Hartford may price this as a 'prior acts buy-back' — get the quote and compare to switching markets. For the immediate term, identify any known wrongful acts pre-8/18/2023 and disclose them now (rather than risk an actual-knowledge dispute later).
discoveryQuestions: When was the PE buyout that brought Lincoln Shields and Black Mountain into the cap table? Are there any board decisions from that period that could be challenged today?
Were you aware that the upper $1M of your D&O has a different (later) prior-acts date than the bottom $1M? Did the broker quote a flat prior-acts date as an option?
Has your HR team had any 2021-2023 employment matters that resolved without a lawsuit? Could any of them re-emerge?
If a derivative action was filed today citing decisions made before August 2023 — would you expect any of your D&O to respond?

findings.requirement_type: Cyber — Continuity Date 4/1/2023 (Insufficient for 50+ Year Company)
findings.contract_quote: ...any retroactive date under the policy shall precede the effective date of this contract and either continuous coverage will be maintained, or an extended discovery period will be exercised for a period of two years beginning at the time work under this contract is completed.
findings.policy_quote: Continuity Date: 04/01/2023
findings.policy_page: AmTrust Cyber Dec page Item 5, p 3
findings.gap_description: Cyber Continuity Date is 4/1/2023 — only 2 years before current policy inception. Maricopa contract effective is 11/1/2021 (per req-003 commentary). The retro is therefore AFTER the contract effective, which violates §8.2.3 ('retroactive date under the policy shall precede the effective date of this contract'). Any cyber event with origin date prior to 4/1/2023 — a persistent threat actor with undetected access dating back further, an unauthorized acquisition of voter data in a prior breach now surfacing, a long-running fraud scheme — is uncovered. For a 50+ year company this is a structural prior-acts gap.
findings.plain_english: Your Cyber policy treats anything that happened before April 1, 2023 as outside the coverage window. The Maricopa contract that started in November 2021 specifically requires the retro to be before the contract started. So the policy is technically out of compliance, and any breach that started in 2022 — like an attacker who has been quietly inside the network — is excluded.
findings.recommendation: At renewal, request continuity date moved back to no later than 11/1/2021 (Maricopa contract effective date) and ideally to date of original incorporation. Where carrier won't move, request 'full prior acts' continuity. Run a compromise assessment to detect any active long-dwell threats now, before they become uninsurable claims.
discoveryQuestions: When did your IT team last conduct a compromise assessment to look for long-dwell threats — the kind that could have been in the network for years?
Did anyone explain that your Cyber Continuity Date is two years AFTER your Maricopa contract started?
If a breach surfaced today and forensic analysis showed first compromise in 2022, do you know whether the policy would cover the resulting claims?

findings.requirement_type: Designated Entity Notice of Cancellation — Sacramento, Maricopa, LA County Missing
findings.contract_quote: Applicable to all insurance policies required within the insurance requirements of this contract, Contractor's insurance shall not be permitted to expire, be suspended, be canceled, or be materially changed for any reason without 30 days prior written notice to Maricopa County.
findings.policy_quote: WC Notice of Cancellation to Designated Entity(s): El Paso County, Coconino County, Amazon.com Services LLC. Auto Notice of Cancellation: BLANKET WHERE REQUIRED BY WRITTEN CONTRACT, City of Boulder, Coconino County, Amazon.com, El Paso County, San Luis Obispo County, State of Colorado, NY State OGS. Hanover Commercial Notice of Cancellation: NY State OGS, Amazon.com, ARC Airport, Banterra Bank.
findings.policy_page: WC Form 331-0342, p 112; Auto Form 401-1235, pp 44-46; Commercial Form 401-1235, p 36
findings.policy_file: Multiple — Hanover WC, Hanover Auto, Hanover Commercial Package

findings.plain_english: Every county contract requires that the County itself receives a 30-day notice if any of your insurance policies cancel. Your insurance policies have a 'designated entity' list — and the counties you actually contract with (Maricopa, Sacramento, LA) aren't on those lists. Some policies don't have designated-entity endorsements at all. This means if a policy got cancelled (for non-payment, for a material change, whatever), the County wouldn't be told — and you'd be in technical breach of contract every day until you fixed it.

Where the carrier won't endorse, fall back on a contractual undertaking from the broker to forward any cancellation notice within 24 hours. Include this fix on the certificate-of-insurance issuance protocol so future contracts don't repeat the gap.
discoveryQuestions: If your Cyber policy got cancelled mid-term for non-payment in October, who would tell Maricopa County?
Has anyone reviewed the existing 'designated entity' lists on your policies and matched them against your active county contracts?
When a county risk manager asks for proof that they'll be notified of cancellation, what document do you send them?

findings.requirement_type: GL — Restrictive Endorsements Violate Sacramento 'No Additional Exclusions' Standard

Including, but not limited to Premises/Operations, Products/Completed Operations, Contractual, and Personal & Advertising Injury, without additional exclusions or limitations, unless approved by the County Risk Manager.
findings.policy_quote: 421-5286 Cyber Incident-Cyber Content Exclusion (page 208); CG 00 69 12 23 Violation of Law Addressing Data Privacy Exclusion (page 226); CG 21 06 12 23 Access or Disclosure of Confidential or Personal Material or Information (page 236); CG 21 49 09 99 Total Pollution Exclusion (page 240); CG 40 32 05 23 PFAS Exclusion (page 252); 421-5203 07 23 Phthalates Exclusion (page 206); CG 21 67 12 04 Fungi or Bacteria Exclusion (page 244); CG 21 73 01 15 Exclusion of Certified Acts of Terrorism (page 246); CG 21 96 03 05 Silica Exclusion (page 248).
findings.gap_description: Sacramento §II.A requires CG 00 01 'without additional exclusions or limitations, unless approved by the County Risk Manager.' The Hanover Commercial GL carries at least nine restrictive endorsements (cyber, data privacy, access/disclosure, total pollution, PFAS, phthalates, fungi, terrorism, silica). None of these have been individually approved by the Sacramento County Risk Manager. The cyber/privacy exclusions are particularly material to the risk profile (election services, voter PII). This is a structural compliance issue with Sacramento County contracts — though most of the exclusions are industry-standard tightening that no carrier omits, Sacramento's contract language gives the County argument for non-compliance.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento's contract says your GL policy can't have any extra exclusions beyond the standard ISO form unless their Risk Manager approves them. Your GL has nine such extra exclusions — most of them are normal industry-standard exclusions that every carrier puts on, but technically you're out of compliance with the contract language. The Risk Manager could push back when reviewing your certificate. Practically, the cyber and data privacy exclusions are the most material, since voter data is your business and those exclusions cut out the most likely modern claim.
findings.recommendation: Two-track response: (1) submit the GL endorsement schedule to Sacramento County Risk Manager for written approval (most counties accept industry-standard exclusions when shown); (2) confirm at next renewal that no carrier-specific narrowing endorsements (e.g., classification limitations, manufacturing carve-outs) have been added. Disclose the cyber/data-privacy exclusions specifically — Sacramento should understand that those exposures are addressed by your separate Cyber policy.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: Cyber/data privacy exclusions are addressed by AmTrust Cyber (subject to Finding 002). Pollution is NOT covered — see Finding 020. PFAS, phthalates, silica, fungi exclusions have no other coverage in the program.
discoveryQuestions: Has the Sacramento County Risk Manager ever signed off on any of the GL endorsements — cyber, pollution, data privacy?
If Sacramento rejects the GL because of these added exclusions, do you know which contracts would be affected and what the financial impact would be?
Do you know which policy in your program is meant to pick up where these GL exclusions leave off?

findings.requirement_type: GL — Maricopa Aggregate Shortfall ($2M Cap vs $4M Required)
findings.contract_quote: Commercial General Liability (CGL) insurance and, if necessary, Commercial Umbrella insurance with a limit of not less than $2,000,000 for each occurrence, $4,000,000 Products/Completed Operations Aggregate, and $4,000,000 General Aggregate Limit.
findings.policy_quote: Each Occurrence: $1,000,000; General Aggregate: $2,000,000; Products Completed Operations Aggregate: Included in General Aggregate (NOT a separate limit); Per-Project/Per-Location Aggregate Cap: $2,000,000 (Form 421-3635).
findings.policy_page: Hanover Commercial CGL Dec, p 18; 421-3635, p 204
findings.gap_description: Maricopa requires $2M each occurrence, $4M Products/Comp Ops Aggregate, $4M Gen Agg, AND specifies that Umbrella may be combined to meet the minimum. Hanover GL is $1M/$2M with Products shared in Gen Agg, capped at $2M policy aggregate. The Hanover Umbrella ($10M) follows form on Coverage A and DOES sit over the Hanover GL — so total per-occurrence capacity is $11M and total aggregate (with umbrella drop-down) is $12M, exceeding Maricopa's $4M/$4M minimum on a combined basis. Maricopa §8.2.9 expressly permits this combination and requires the COI to identify which lines the umbrella covers. So compliance requires the COI to call out the umbrella as satisfying the $2M occurrence and $4M aggregate minimums for GL — verify your COI does this. Sacramento §III.A demands separate $2M Gen Agg and $2M Products/Comp Ops, which your GL does not separately structure (shared); umbrella drop-down again provides cover but the COI must reflect.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa wants $2M per claim and $4M total per year for general liability. Your primary GL is $1M per claim and $2M total. On its own, the GL is short. But Maricopa specifically allows you to count your Umbrella, and your $10M Umbrella sits on top — combined, you're well above the requirement. The catch is that your certificate of insurance must clearly tell the County that the Umbrella stacks with the GL. If your COI doesn't say so, Maricopa can technically refuse the certificate.
findings.recommendation: Pull a current COI and verify the umbrella is identified as covering the underlying GL. Where Sacramento and Maricopa-specific certificates are needed, add language explicitly stating the $10M Umbrella is excess of CGL/Auto/EL and identifying the per-occurrence and aggregate satisfaction. Consider buying back a separate Products/Completed Operations aggregate at the primary GL layer to reduce reliance on umbrella drop-down for products claims (more meaningful for a manufacturer than a typical service firm).
findings.covered_by_which_policy: Hanover Umbrella ($10M follow-form excess) — combined limits comfortably exceed both contracts' minimums. COI must affirmatively identify Umbrella attachment per Maricopa §8.2.9.
discoveryQuestions: Does the COI you send to Maricopa specifically identify the Umbrella as sitting over the CGL with $2M occurrence / $4M aggregate?
Did anyone explain that your per-project/per-location aggregate is capped at $2M policy aggregate — meaning the per-project benefit is limited?
Are there scenarios where you'd want the Products/Completed Ops aggregate separate from General — for example, if you printed a defective ballot that triggered multiple county claims?

findings.requirement_type: Auto — Maricopa CSL Shortfall ($1M vs $2M Required)
findings.contract_quote: Commercial/Business Automobile Liability insurance with a combined single limit for bodily injury and property damage of not less than $2,000,000 each occurrence with respect to any of the Contractor's owned, hired, and non-owned vehicles...
findings.policy_quote: Liability Combined Single Limit: $1,000,000
findings.gap_description: Hanover Auto carries $1M CSL — half of Maricopa's $2M requirement. The Hanover Umbrella follows form to Auto via Coverage A and sits over $1M CSL, providing combined capacity of $11M. Owned vehicles (2013 Mercedes Sprinter, 2018 Chevrolet Express), hired auto coverage (cost-of-hire basis, AZ class 6611), and non-owned auto (55 employees, AZ class 6602) all confirmed.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa wants $2 million in combined auto liability; you carry $1 million. Your $10M Umbrella stacks on top, getting you to $11M combined — which satisfies the contract — but only if the certificate of insurance you send to Maricopa explicitly identifies the Umbrella as covering Auto.
findings.recommendation: Confirm the Maricopa-issued COI shows Umbrella attaching over Auto. As a practical matter, a $1M primary auto on a fleet of just two vehicles (plus hired/non-owned) is on the lower end for a $5M-$25M revenue company; consider increasing primary Auto to $2M at next renewal to remove dependence on umbrella drop-down for automobile claims and reduce attritional erosion of umbrella aggregate.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: Hanover Umbrella ($10M follow-form excess). COI must identify umbrella attachment per Maricopa §8.2.9.
discoveryQuestions: How many vehicles do your employees actually drive on county business — owned, leased, or their own personal cars?
If a Runbeck driver caused a serious bodily injury accident on the way to a polling place, do you know whether the $1M primary or the umbrella would respond first?
Has the Maricopa County risk manager ever pushed back on the auto certificate?

findings.requirement_type: Auto — Named Driver Exclusion (Malina Trujillo)
findings.contract_quote: Commercial Automobile Liability for Corporate/business owned vehicles including non-owned and hired, $1,000,000 Combined Single Limit.
findings.policy_quote: Excludes coverage for any 'accident' or 'loss' resulting from operation/use of any covered auto by Malina Trujillo (with exception of UM/UIM).
findings.policy_page: Endorsement 461-0425 (9/10) Arizona Exclusion of Named Driver, p 8

The exclusion is typically requested when the carrier identifies the named individual as a high-risk driver via MVR pull. Per CLAUDE.md rule 8 (ask WHY), the underwriter likely had a legitimate reason — but Run-Test should know whether this individual has any operational connection to the company.
findings.plain_english: Your Auto policy specifically excludes any coverage for accidents caused by an individual named Malina Trujillo. If this person is an employee, contractor, or family member of an officer who has access to company vehicles — and they get into an accident — there is no insurance. This is a name-specific, surgical exclusion the carrier asked for. Verify whether this person has any current connection to Run-Test operations.
findings.recommendation: Verify with HR whether Malina Trujillo is a current or former employee, and whether they have ever operated a company vehicle. Confirm that fleet keys are not accessible to this individual. If the individual is no longer associated with the company, request removal of the exclusion at next renewal. Document the policy in the driver-vetting protocol so this risk does not silently re-emerge.
discoveryQuestions: Is Malina Trujillo a current or former Runbeck employee, contractor, or family member of management? How did this person end up named on the auto policy?
What is your protocol for issuing keys or vehicle access to new employees, and how does it tie back to MVR pulls and the named-driver exclusion list?

findings.requirement_type: Property — Valuable Papers Sublimit Inadequate for Election Records
findings.contract_quote: [No specific contract requirement on Property/Inland Marine — but service-line risk requires]
findings.policy_quote: Cost to replace/restore information on valuable papers and records (deeds, manuscripts, books of account, abstracts, drawings, card index systems) excluded from Covered Property. Limited Coverage Extension provides only $2,500 per premises unless higher limit shown.
findings.gap_description: BPP form treats Valuable Papers as excluded property except for a $2,500 Coverage Extension. Run-Test maintains physical voter records, ballot logs, signature data, and election certifications across operations. A fire, water-loss, or vandalism event affecting these records could easily exceed $2,500 in restoration cost (though most modern election records are also digitized — verify backup protocols). The base BPP also caps Electronic Data restoration at $2,500/year. Recommend a Valuable Papers and Records (VP&R) endorsement raising this sublimit to $250,000+ aligned with the volume of physical records maintained.
findings.plain_english: Your Property policy will only spend $2,500 restoring damaged election records — paper ballots in storage, signature logs, voter rolls in physical form. For an election services company, that's a token amount. A small fire or water leak in a records-storage area could easily consume hundreds of thousands of dollars in scanning, re-creation, and re-certification costs.
findings.recommendation: Add a Valuable Papers and Records endorsement with a per-occurrence limit aligned to the physical-records volume (typical: $250K–$1M). Audit your records-management protocols: which categories of records are paper-only, which are digitized with backup, and what restoration would actually cost. Consider Inland Marine Valuable Papers schedule for off-site/transit exposure.
discoveryQuestions: How many physical election records does Runbeck have in storage at any given time, and where are they kept?
If your records storage area suffered a sprinkler activation, what would it cost to scan and re-create the documents?
Did the broker run a Valuable Papers analysis for a vendor handling election records — and recommend a sublimit higher than $2,500?

findings.requirement_type: Equipment Breakdown — Programming/Virus/Data Loss Carve-Out
findings.contract_quote: [No specific contract requirement — operational risk finding]
findings.policy_quote: An 'accident' under EB does NOT include defect, programming error, programming limitation, computer virus, malicious code, loss of 'data', loss of access, loss of use, loss of functionality. Also excludes misalignment, miscalibration, tripping off-line, or any condition correctable by reset/cleaning/maintenance.
findings.gap_description: Equipment Breakdown carries a $49M limit, signaling a fleet of high-value election technology equipment (ballot scanners, sorters, printers, mail processing systems). The form expressly excludes loss caused by programming error, computer virus, malicious code, loss of data, or loss of functionality — exactly the failure modes most relevant to election technology. A ransomware attack that bricks a sorter is excluded. A software update that misaligns a scanner is excluded. The Cyber policy's Bricking Costs sublimit ($4M aggregate, shared) becomes the only fallback — and that aggregate is shared with 13 other coverages.
findings.plain_english: Your Equipment Breakdown coverage covers $49 million of election technology equipment — but only when the equipment fails the old-fashioned way (motor burns out, capacitor pops). If your ballot sorter gets bricked by a software update, ransomware, a corrupted firmware patch, or a programming error, the Equipment Breakdown policy says no. Your Cyber policy's Bricking coverage is supposed to fill that gap, but the Cyber tower is undersized and shared across many coverages.
findings.recommendation: Two paths: (1) negotiate at renewal a 'cyber-related Equipment Breakdown' carve-back tying programming/virus loss back into EB coverage (some carriers offer this as a sub-line); or (2) ensure the Cyber tower includes a dedicated Bricking sublimit equal to or above your highest-value piece of equipment, with sufficient aggregate to absorb a multi-equipment incident.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: AmTrust Cyber Bricking Costs ($4M shared aggregate, defense within limits) — but undersized given EB exposure.
discoveryQuestions: What is the most expensive piece of election processing equipment you operate, and what would it cost to replace if it got bricked by ransomware?
Did the broker explain that your $49M Equipment Breakdown coverage doesn't apply to ransomware, software updates, or programming errors?
Have you had any near-miss equipment events caused by software issues, and how did you resolve them?

findings.requirement_type: Inland Marine — Missing for Election Equipment in Transit
findings.contract_quote: Any Inland Marine insurance policies maintained by the CONTRACTOR in performance of the Agreement shall be endorsed to state that the insurer shall waive all rights of subrogation against the COUNTY.
findings.policy_quote: [No standalone Inland Marine policy in the program. Hanover Commercial Property provides BPP In Transit $100K and BPP Off Premises $250K only.]
findings.gap_description: Sacramento §IX explicitly contemplates that Run-Test maintains Inland Marine coverage — and requires Waiver of Subrogation if it does. There is no standalone Inland Marine policy in the program. The Hanover Commercial Property covers BPP In Transit at only $100K and BPP Off Premises at $250K — wholly inadequate for transporting election technology equipment between Run-Test's Phoenix HQ and county locations across 31+ states. Election sorters, scanners, and high-volume printers can each exceed $100K-$500K. A single truck rollover en route to a county election site could exhaust the in-transit coverage on one piece of equipment. Per Hanover Commercial endorsements, the only specialty IM-style coverage is the limited 'Property Off Premises' $250K and 'BPP In Transit' $100K under the Property form; no scheduled equipment, motor-truck cargo, contractors equipment, or installation floater.
findings.plain_english: When you ship a high-speed ballot sorter or scanner to a county for an election, that piece of equipment is in transit — moving across multiple states. Your Property policy gives you only $100,000 of coverage for property in transit. A single piece of election equipment can be worth more than that. If a truck rolls over carrying two sorters, you're underinsured by hundreds of thousands of dollars. There is no standalone Inland Marine policy in your program. Sacramento County's contract specifically anticipates you have Inland Marine — and you don't.
findings.recommendation: Place a Contractors Equipment / Installation Floater Inland Marine policy with: (1) blanket scheduled equipment limit equal to the highest single piece-of-equipment value; (2) in-transit limit at full equipment value (not just $100K); (3) installation floater for equipment installed at county sites until accepted; (4) blanket Waiver of Subrogation per Sacramento §IX. Also include Motor Truck Cargo if Run-Test self-transports.
discoveryQuestions: How do you transport election sorters and scanners from Phoenix to county sites — own truck, common carrier, equipment-leasing company?
What is the value of your largest single piece of equipment, and what's typically on a truck at one time?
If a truck rolled over en route to Sacramento County carrying two sorters, do you know what your insurance pays?
Has anyone done a per-shipment maximum-value-at-risk calculation for your equipment movements?

findings.requirement_type: Pollution — Total Pollution Exclusion + No CPL in Program
findings.contract_quote: [No specific contract requirement — operational risk finding triggered by pollution exposures in printing/manufacturing operations]
findings.policy_quote: Hanover GL: Total Pollution Exclusion (CG 21 49 09 99, p 240). Hanover Umbrella: Total Pollution Exclusion (475-0027, p 44 — Coverage A). Gemini Tech E&O: Pollution, Asbestos and Lead (Absolute) — VP 00 06 10 17 §IV.J, p 9. Arch Security GL: Total Pollution Exclusion with Hostile Fire and Self-Defense Spray Exception (00 GL1047 00 01 25, p 21).
findings.policy_file: Multiple — Hanover Commercial, Hanover Umbrella, Gemini E&O, Arch Security GL
findings.gap_description: Every liability policy in the program excludes pollution. Run-Test operates a printing/mailing manufacturing facility — toner spills, ink leaks, solvent releases, paper dust, and chemical fume incidents are all within the operational footprint. There is no Contractors Pollution Liability or Site Pollution Liability in the program. The only carve-back is on the Arch Security Guards GL (hostile fire and self-defense spray) — irrelevant to manufacturing pollution. A toner dump in a county facility, ink contamination of voter records, or a chemical spill in the Phoenix HQ would be uninsured. Note: this is a manufacturing operation per the client profile — phthalates and PFAS exclusions on the GL further narrow chemical-related coverage.
findings.plain_english: Your General Liability, Umbrella, and Tech E&O all exclude pollution. You run a printing operation that uses inks, toners, solvents, and chemicals. If toner spills at a county warehouse, if ink contaminates a building's air handling system, if a chemical leak damages property — none of your policies pay. Manufacturing-style pollution claims aren't huge but they happen, and right now you have nothing in the program to absorb them.
findings.recommendation: Place a Contractors Pollution Liability (CPL) / Site Pollution Liability policy. Typical limits: $1M-$2M per claim, $2M-$5M aggregate. Form should cover: on-site pollution at owned/leased premises; off-site pollution at customer locations during ballot/equipment delivery; indoor air-quality claims; and transportation pollution. Cost: typically $5K-$15K for a printing/mailing operation of this size.
discoveryQuestions: What chemicals, inks, toners, and solvents do your printing operations use? What's the largest single container on site at any time?
Have you ever had a near-miss spill or leak — even something minor that you cleaned up internally?
If toner contaminated the air handling system at a county site you were servicing, who would pay the remediation?

findings.requirement_type: Hartford Workplace Violence — No Third-Party Liability
findings.contract_quote: [No specific contract requirement — operational risk finding]
findings.policy_quote: Workplace Violence coverage is EXPENSE coverage only (BI, employee, PR firm). Endorsement EXPLICITLY excludes 'any legal costs, attorneys fees, expenses, settlements, judgments, penalties or other amounts incurred as a result of any claim, suit or other legal proceeding brought against an Insured in connection with a Workplace Violence Action.'
findings.gap_description: The Hartford EPLI Workplace Violence endorsement provides $100K of expense coverage (BI for employees, PR firm, security consultant) but EXPRESSLY EXCLUDES third-party liability arising from workplace violence (lawsuits, settlements, judgments). Election services facilities are politically sensitive targets; ballot processing centers have been the subject of both threats and actual incidents in recent election cycles. A third-party shooting victim or family member suing Run-Test for negligent security, premises liability, or failure to warn would NOT be covered by the Workplace Violence endorsement — they would have to be covered (if at all) by GL.
findings.plain_english: Your Workplace Violence coverage pays for hospital bills, counseling, PR firms, and security after a violent event — but it does not pay for the lawsuits that follow. If a victim's family sues you for inadequate security, settlements come out of your General Liability — and the GL has its own assault and battery limitations and politicized-environment risk. Election processing facilities have become political targets; this gap deserves attention.
findings.recommendation: At renewal, request a buy-up of third-party liability under the Workplace Violence endorsement, OR confirm that Hanover GL's assault & battery treatment is broad enough to cover a workplace shooting scenario (the Arch Security Guards GL has assault & battery coverage but it's a separate monoline; the primary Hanover GL doesn't have a similar carve-back). Consider a standalone Active Assailant / Workplace Violence policy from a specialty carrier (Beazley, AIG, Munich Re) — typical $1M-$5M limits with both expense and third-party liability.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: Partial — Hanover Commercial GL would respond to third-party premises liability, but base ISO CG 00 01 has expected/intended exclusion for workplace violence (the Arch Security Guards GL has an assault/battery carve-back but only applies to security operations, not Run-Test's election services).
discoveryQuestions: Has Runbeck implemented workplace violence prevention training, security audits, or threat assessment programs after the heightened election environment of 2020-2024?
Do you feel confident that if a violent event happened at the Phoenix processing center, your insurance would cover the inevitable wave of lawsuits?
Have you ever received specific threats targeting your operations or staff?

findings.requirement_type: Hartford Crime — Social Engineering Sublimit ($15K Token)
findings.contract_quote: [Maricopa cyber spec requires social engineering coverage — but the Crime program is separate]
findings.policy_quote: Crime Deception Fraud / Social Engineering: $15,000 limit
findings.gap_description: Hartford Crime has $2M Computer/Funds Transfer Fraud, $2M Employee Theft, $2M Forgery — all robust limits — but Deception Fraud (social engineering) is sublimited to $15,000. Combined with the AmTrust Cyber Cyber Deception phantom coverage ($250K limit / $250K retention = $0 effective), the program-wide social engineering capacity is roughly $15K-$265K in the worst case. For an election services vendor whose finance team handles county invoices, vendor payables, and mid-six-figure wire transfers, this is materially inadequate.
findings.plain_english: Your Crime policy covers $2 million for traditional computer fraud — where a hacker breaks into your network and moves money. But it covers only $15,000 for social engineering — where a fraudster tricks an employee into authorizing a payment. Modern wire fraud is overwhelmingly social engineering, not network intrusion. The $15K sublimit on Crime, combined with the phantom Cyber Deception coverage, leaves the program almost wholly exposed to wire-fraud schemes.
findings.recommendation: At renewal, increase Crime social engineering / deception fraud sublimit to match the broader Crime limits ($1M-$2M). Most carriers offer this as a buy-up for modest premium. Pair with payment-control protocols (dual approval, out-of-band verification) that often unlock better terms.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: AmTrust Cyber Cyber Deception ($250K/$250K — phantom). Combined real-world capacity is $15K Crime + $0 Cyber on losses ≤ $250K = $15K total.
discoveryQuestions: What's the largest wire transfer your AP team processes in a typical month?
Did the broker explain to you that your Social Engineering / Deception Fraud sublimit is only $15,000?
How many vendors and county AP departments does your finance team interact with electronically each month?

findings.requirement_type: Hartford Crime — Theft of Confidential Information / IP / Voter Data Excluded
findings.contract_quote: [Voter PII protection is core risk — Maricopa cyber spec contemplates first-party theft of data]
findings.policy_quote: No coverage for theft/disclosure of trade secrets, IP, credit card numbers, bank account numbers, etc. (unless covered under IA 8 Identity Recovery), or Data (unless covered under IA 7).
findings.gap_description: The Hartford Crime policy explicitly excludes loss arising from theft of confidential information, IP, credit card numbers, bank account numbers, etc. Run-Test handles voter PII for 90M+ registered voters. Theft of voter data by an employee — the classic insider threat scenario — is NOT a Crime claim but pushed entirely to Cyber. With Cyber undersized and shared aggregate, the insider data-theft exposure is materially under-covered.
findings.plain_english: If a Runbeck employee steals voter PII and sells it on the dark web, your Crime policy says no — Crime only covers theft of money or physical property, not data. The claim falls to Cyber, which is too small. Insider data-theft is among the most damaging scenarios for an election services company, and your program treats it as a Cyber-only risk that the Cyber tower can't fully absorb.
findings.recommendation: Cure two ways: (1) increase Cyber tower per Finding 002; (2) confirm Hartford Crime Identity Recovery (IA 8) and Computer Systems Restoration (IA 7) limits are aligned with insider-threat scenarios. Implement insider-threat program controls (privileged access management, data-loss prevention monitoring, exit-employee data audit) — many cyber carriers offer premium credits for these controls.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: AmTrust Cyber — Privacy & Network Security ($4M shared aggregate). Insufficient — see Finding 002.
discoveryQuestions: How does your security team monitor for insider data exfiltration — particularly for employees who handle voter databases?
If a departing employee was suspected of taking voter data with them, what would the response cost — investigation, notification, regulatory defense?
Did anyone explain that insider data theft falls to Cyber — not Crime — under your current program?

findings.requirement_type: Hartford ML — Antitrust Sublimit (D&O)
findings.contract_quote: [No contract requirement — operational risk finding for an election services market participant]
findings.policy_quote: Antitrust/Sherman/Clayton/FTC violations subject to sublimit of lesser of remaining limit or $1,000,000.
findings.gap_description: D&O includes a sublimit of $1M for Antitrust/Sherman/Clayton/FTC violations — a carve-back from full exclusion. The election services market is consolidating; antitrust scrutiny has been a feature of recent industry M&A. findings.plain_english: If your D&O is sued for antitrust — a competitor accusing Runbeck of monopolistic conduct in the election services market, or a federal investigation — your insurance pays up to $1 million. Antitrust litigation routinely costs more than $1 million in defense costs alone.
findings.recommendation: At renewal, evaluate carriers that don't impose this sublimit, or buy back full antitrust coverage if available. Cost of buy-back is typically modest for a private company without prior antitrust history.
discoveryQuestions: Has Runbeck been involved in any antitrust complaints, FTC inquiries, or competitor disputes in the last five years?
Did the broker explain that antitrust claims are sublimited to $1M, even though the rest of D&O is $2M?
How many election services vendors compete for your typical county RFPs — and how does the market structure look from a regulator's perspective?

findings.requirement_type: EBL — Cyber/Programming/Virus Carve-Out
findings.contract_quote: [Operational risk — EBL is a specific coverage]
findings.policy_quote: EDP coverage excludes errors/omissions in programming, electrical disturbance, power supply disturbance, computer virus, and computer hacking
findings.gap_description: Employee Benefits Liability ($1M/$1M) within the Hanover Commercial Package has a retroactive date of 4/8/2017. EBL covers administrative errors in benefits enrollment, eligibility, and plan administration. The EDP-related carve-outs limit coverage when an employee benefits issue stems from a software glitch in HR systems.
